question_text: A user device computes its timing advance from satellite ephemeris and its own GNSS position, and applies it before sending its first preamble. Which stage of the correction chain is this?
options: Open-loop timing advance
Closed-loop frequency offset compensation
The Timing Advance command procedure
Residual tracking by the numerically controlled oscillator
correct_answer: Open-loop timing advance
explanation: Open loop means proactive: the device predicts the correction from geometry it already knows, and applies it before it has ever transmitted. The closed loop only starts once the network has measured a real uplink.
topic: Timing advance and frequency offset compensation in LEO NTN

question_text: Why can closed-loop timing advance never remove the timing error completely?
options: The MAC control element cannot carry a large enough correction value
The correction is based on geometry that is at least one round trip old
The base station measures arrival time with limited resolution only
The satellite clock and the device clock use different time references
correct_answer: The correction is based on geometry that is at least one round trip old
explanation: Feedback always trails the true geometry by at least one round trip. On a LEO link the geometry moves during that round trip, so a residual error is left behind no matter how accurate the measurement was.
topic: Timing advance and frequency offset compensation in LEO NTN

question_text: In a transparent payload the end-to-end Doppler is roughly double that of the service link alone. What causes the doubling?
options: The uplink and the downlink carriers are at different frequencies
The signal is sampled twice, once on board and once at the gateway
The feeder link between the satellite and the gateway adds its own shift
Inter-satellite links re-transmit the signal to a second spacecraft
correct_answer: The feeder link between the satellite and the gateway adds its own shift
explanation: A transparent payload does not demodulate. The signal crosses the service link and then the feeder link, and each moving segment contributes a Doppler shift, so the two add.
topic: Timing advance and frequency offset compensation in LEO NTN

question_text: The device predicts Doppler as fD = (Vr / c) x fc. What does Vr stand for?
options: The full orbital speed of the satellite
The ground speed of the user device
The rate at which the elevation angle is changing
The component of relative velocity along the line of sight
correct_answer: The component of relative velocity along the line of sight
explanation: Doppler responds only to the closing or opening rate along the line of sight. At the zenith of a pass the satellite is moving fast but almost none of that motion is radial, so the shift crosses zero.
topic: Timing advance and frequency offset compensation in LEO NTN

question_text: Which pair of inputs does the open-loop stage need before the device has transmitted anything at all?
options: Satellite ephemeris and the device's own GNSS position
A Timing Advance command and an AFC error estimate
Received signal strength and the current beam identity
Feeder link Doppler and the gateway clock offset
correct_answer: Satellite ephemeris and the device's own GNSS position
explanation: Two positions give a range, and a range gives a delay and a radial velocity. Everything else in the list is either a measurement the network has not made yet or a quantity the device cannot see.
topic: Timing advance and frequency offset compensation in LEO NTN

question_text: A stale ephemeris file degrades performance. Which stage suffers first and worst?
options: The closed loop, because the correction command becomes invalid
The open loop, because its prediction is built on the orbit data
Neither, because GNSS timing overrides the ephemeris
Both equally, because they share the same estimate
correct_answer: The open loop, because its prediction is built on the orbit data
explanation: The open loop is pure prediction from the orbit, so bad orbit data corrupts it directly. The closed loop measures the real signal, so it is the stage that partly rescues a stale prediction.
topic: Timing advance and frequency offset compensation in LEO NTN

question_text: What is the stated cost of issuing timing advance commands and AFC updates frequently?
options: The device battery drains faster than the payload can support
The satellite must carry a larger soft buffer
Uplink and downlink capacity is spent that could otherwise carry data
The cyclic prefix must be lengthened for every user
correct_answer: Uplink and downlink capacity is spent that could otherwise carry data
explanation: Corrections are signalling, and signalling occupies the same radio resources as user traffic. Correcting more often buys accuracy and pays for it in throughput.
topic: Timing advance and frequency offset compensation in LEO NTN

question_text: Which correction is the network side, rather than the device side, responsible for?
options: Service link Doppler pre-compensation
The initial timing advance before the first PRACH
The GNSS position fix used in the open loop
Feeder link Doppler and the residual measurement
correct_answer: Feeder link Doppler and the residual measurement
explanation: The split follows what each end can observe. The device sees its own service link and pre-corrects it. Only the network sees the feeder link and the residual error in the arriving signal.
topic: Timing advance and frequency offset compensation in LEO NTN

question_text: Compared with a terrestrial cell link, the round-trip time on a LEO link is best described as:
options: Long and fast-changing
Short and stable
Long but essentially constant over a pass
Short but highly variable
correct_answer: Long and fast-changing
explanation: Both properties matter. Length alone could be absorbed by a fixed offset. It is the fact that the length keeps changing during a pass that forces a continuous correction loop.
topic: Timing advance and frequency offset compensation in LEO NTN

question_text: Which statement captures the design pattern shared by timing advance and frequency offset compensation?
options: Measure first, then predict the next value from the measurement history
Predict from known geometry, then refine from real measurement
Let the network compute everything and broadcast one common value
Avoid prediction entirely and rely on a long cyclic prefix
correct_answer: Predict from known geometry, then refine from real measurement
explanation: This is the open-loop then closed-loop pattern stated in the conclusion. Prediction gets the device close enough to be heard at all; measurement closes the remaining gap.
topic: Timing advance and frequency offset compensation in LEO NTN

question_text: Why does a UAV base station need beam steering in elevation, when a terrestrial macro cell largely does not?
options: Elevation steering is required to reduce Doppler on the feeder link
The users lie below the platform, so the useful angles are vertical as well as horizontal
Regulations cap the azimuth beamwidth of airborne transmitters
Elevation steering compensates for the rotation of the Earth
correct_answer: The users lie below the platform, so the useful angles are vertical as well as horizontal
explanation: A tower stands among its users, so the interesting variation is horizontal. A UAV hovers above them, so the angle down to a user changes with range, and elevation becomes a real steering axis.
topic: UAV-enhanced 3D beamforming for rural 5G NTN

question_text: What is the main engineering reason for choosing hybrid beamforming rather than fully digital beamforming on a UAV?
options: It gives a wider beam, which tolerates platform tilt better
It removes the need for any baseband processing on board
It uses fewer RF chains than antenna elements, which saves size, weight and power
It allows the UAV to serve users on more than one carrier frequency
correct_answer: It uses fewer RF chains than antenna elements, which saves size, weight and power
explanation: A fully digital array needs one RF chain per element. Hybrid beamforming puts a digital precoder behind an analog phase-shift network, so a large array is driven by a small number of chains, which is what an aircraft can lift and power.
topic: UAV-enhanced 3D beamforming for rural 5G NTN

question_text: The control loop runs sense, optimize, act, learn. Which weakness does this loop introduce?
options: It cannot handle users that stay in one place for long periods
It requires every user device to run the same learning model
It prevents the UAV from changing altitude once deployed
Convergence takes time, so link quality dips during fast movement
correct_answer: Convergence takes time, so link quality dips during fast movement
explanation: A closed learning loop is always chasing the state it last observed. When the geometry changes faster than the loop converges, the beam is briefly aimed at where the users were rather than where they are.
topic: UAV-enhanced 3D beamforming for rural 5G NTN

question_text: Predictive beam tracking is preferred over repeated exhaustive beam search mainly because:
options: It holds alignment without the overhead of re-searching every beam
Exhaustive search cannot find the correct beam at high elevation angles
Prediction removes the need for a phase-shift network
Exhaustive search is forbidden by the 3GPP NTN specification
correct_answer: It holds alignment without the overhead of re-searching every beam
explanation: Sweeping every beam costs time and signalling on every update. Predicting the next weights from the motion already observed reaches the same alignment for a fraction of that overhead.
topic: UAV-enhanced 3D beamforming for rural 5G NTN

question_text: In the multi-tier backhaul, what carries traffic out of the target area?
options: A new fibre spur laid to the nearest terrestrial exchange
Inter-UAV mesh links leading up to a HAPS or satellite feeder link
A dedicated ground tower built at the edge of the coverage zone
Direct device-to-device relaying between the rural user terminals
correct_answer: Inter-UAV mesh links leading up to a HAPS or satellite feeder link
explanation: The whole point is to avoid building anything on the ground. UAVs relay to each other and then upward, so no fibre and no tower is needed inside the target area.
topic: UAV-enhanced 3D beamforming for rural 5G NTN

question_text: Altitude is treated as a decision variable rather than a fixed setting. Which trade-off does it control?
options: Transmit power against receiver noise figure
Beam count against subcarrier spacing
Line-of-sight probability against path loss
Backhaul latency against onboard storage
correct_answer: Line-of-sight probability against path loss
explanation: Climbing improves the chance of a clear path over terrain and buildings, and at the same time lengthens every link. The best altitude is wherever those two effects balance for the terrain below.
topic: UAV-enhanced 3D beamforming for rural 5G NTN

question_text: Which limitation is described as competing directly with the UAV's endurance?
options: The weight of the antenna array on its own
The bandwidth reserved for the feeder link
The time taken to compute the digital precoder weights
The power drawn by the beamforming hardware and the AI control loop
correct_answer: The power drawn by the beamforming hardware and the AI control loop
explanation: On an aircraft the payload and the propulsion draw from one battery. Every watt spent on phase shifters and inference is a watt not spent staying airborne.
topic: UAV-enhanced 3D beamforming for rural 5G NTN

question_text: Backhaul fragility is listed as a risk. What is the specific failure mode?
options: One weak link in the chain degrades coverage for everything downstream of it
Two UAVs transmit on the same beam and interfere
The satellite feeder link exceeds its power flux density mask
The mesh loses time synchronisation and the beams misalign
correct_answer: One weak link in the chain degrades coverage for everything downstream of it
explanation: A multi-tier mesh is a chain of dependencies. A UAV that relays through a neighbour inherits that neighbour's problems, so a single weak hop cascades outward.
topic: UAV-enhanced 3D beamforming for rural 5G NTN

question_text: Which of these is given as a real-world application of the approach?
options: Precision timing distribution for financial trading networks
Temporary coverage for festivals and other large events
Space debris tracking from a UAV-borne radar
Inter-continental undersea cable protection monitoring
correct_answer: Temporary coverage for festivals and other large events
explanation: The listed cases are rural education and distance learning, temporary event coverage, border surveillance and post-disaster response. All four share a need for coverage that appears and then goes away.
topic: UAV-enhanced 3D beamforming for rural 5G NTN

question_text: The conclusion argues that the binding constraint is system-level. What does that mean in practice?
options: The UAV must be replaced by a HAPS for the system to work
Only the weakest single radio link needs to be improved
Altitude, beam accuracy, terrain and backhaul have to be optimized together
The AI model must be trained on data from the exact deployment site
correct_answer: Altitude, beam accuracy, terrain and backhaul have to be optimized together
explanation: Improving one variable in isolation moves the bottleneck rather than removing it. Flying higher helps line of sight and hurts path loss, so the variables have to be solved jointly.
topic: UAV-enhanced 3D beamforming for rural 5G NTN

question_text: Why is the four-step RACH handshake especially costly over a satellite link?
options: Each of the four messages must be encrypted separately
The preamble has to be repeated once per orbital plane
The four messages amount to two full satellite round trips before any data moves
The base station cannot process message 3 while in view of the user
correct_answer: The four messages amount to two full satellite round trips before any data moves
explanation: Messages 1 and 2 are one round trip and messages 3 and 4 are another. On the ground that is about a millisecond. Over a satellite it is tens of milliseconds spent before a single byte of user data has been sent.
topic: Machine learning for RACH optimization in NTN

question_text: Differential delay across a narrow LEO beam is about 650 microseconds, and the longest protective cyclic prefix is 684 microseconds. What does that imply?
options: The cyclic prefix is comfortably oversized for LEO operation
Differential delay can be ignored because it sits below the prefix length
Two preambles must be sent, one for the centre and one for the edge
Only about 34 microseconds of margin remains, and wider beams erase it
correct_answer: Only about 34 microseconds of margin remains, and wider beams erase it
explanation: The two figures nearly cancel. The guard barely covers the spread today, so any wider beam or higher orbit pushes edge preambles outside the window entirely.
topic: Machine learning for RACH optimization in NTN

question_text: What happens when two devices pick the same PRACH preamble?
options: A collision occurs, and both devices must retry one round trip later
The network serves the stronger device and silently drops the weaker one
The preambles combine and the base station decodes both correctly
The base station shortens the backoff window for both devices
correct_answer: A collision occurs, and both devices must retry one round trip later
explanation: The preamble is the only thing distinguishing one attempt from another, so identical preambles are indistinguishable. Both attempts fail and both devices pay a full round trip to try again.
topic: Machine learning for RACH optimization in NTN

question_text: Doppler over one LEO pass swings from about +48 kHz to about -48 kHz. What does this do to the RACH?
options: The device is barred from transmitting during the sign reversal
The preamble is smeared, so correlation at the receiver degrades
The random access response arrives on the wrong subcarrier
The cyclic prefix is stretched by the frequency change
correct_answer: The preamble is smeared, so correlation at the receiver degrades
explanation: Preamble detection is a correlation against a known shape. A frequency offset that moves during the preamble distorts that shape, so the correlation peak drops and detections are missed.
topic: Machine learning for RACH optimization in NTN

question_text: In the learning loop, what does the reward signal combine?
options: Beam index, elevation angle and slant range
Collision count, subcarrier spacing and preamble length
Success, delay and energy
Throughput, ephemeris age and satellite battery state
correct_answer: Success, delay and energy
explanation: The reward has to express what a good access attempt looks like: it got through, it did not take long, and it did not cost much power. The policy is then tuned to maximise that combination.
topic: Machine learning for RACH optimization in NTN

question_text: The predictive or ephemeris-aided family is described differently from the other two. Why?
options: It runs only on the satellite and never on the device
It requires far more training data than the other families
It has been shown to perform worse than fixed 3GPP parameters
It is deterministic geometry, and it is the Release 17 baseline that a learned policy must beat
correct_answer: It is deterministic geometry, and it is the Release 17 baseline that a learned policy must beat
explanation: Supervised learning and reinforcement learning both learn from data. Pre-compensating from a known orbit learns nothing; it computes. That makes it the benchmark rather than a competing learned method.
topic: Machine learning for RACH optimization in NTN

question_text: Reinforcement learning is applied to which RACH parameters?
options: The barring probability, the backoff window and the preamble pool split
The carrier frequency and the subcarrier spacing
The cyclic prefix length and the guard period
The number of HARQ processes and the soft buffer size
correct_answer: The barring probability, the backoff window and the preamble pool split
explanation: These are the contention controls, the values a network operator would otherwise fix at design time. They are exactly the knobs a policy can turn in response to observed load.
topic: Machine learning for RACH optimization in NTN

question_text: The reported eRACH result includes a factor of 4.94. What does it measure?
options: The improvement in throughput over fixed rules
The increase in collision rate, which is the cost paid for the gain
The reduction in access delay
The growth in the number of devices that can be served
correct_answer: The increase in collision rate, which is the cost paid for the gain
explanation: The gains quoted are +31.2 percent and +54.6 percent throughput and 1.49 times lower delay. The 4.94 figure runs the other way: the learned policy is more aggressive, so it collides more often.
topic: Machine learning for RACH optimization in NTN

question_text: Why is heat listed as an onboard limitation separate from power?
options: Heat corrupts the stored neural network weights
Thermal noise raises the false preamble detection rate
Onboard inference generates heat with no way to vent it in vacuum
Heat causes the solar panels to lose efficiency during eclipse
correct_answer: Onboard inference generates heat with no way to vent it in vacuum
explanation: On the ground a processor sheds heat into the air. In vacuum there is no convection, so the only path is radiation, and continuous inference produces heat faster than a small payload can radiate it.
topic: Machine learning for RACH optimization in NTN

question_text: Which design-process limitation makes regulatory approval difficult?
options: The scarcity of real NTN random-access traces
The gap between simulated and real channels
The cost of running simulations across many orbital geometries
A black-box policy is hard to certify against 3GPP conformance
correct_answer: A black-box policy is hard to certify against 3GPP conformance
explanation: The other three are engineering obstacles that better data or more compute would ease. Certification is different: a learned policy has no fixed behaviour to test against a written specification.
topic: Machine learning for RACH optimization in NTN

question_text: What is the essential difference between DGPS and PPP?
options: DGPS uses carrier phase while PPP uses code measurements only
DGPS corrects the ionosphere while PPP corrects the troposphere
DGPS works globally while PPP is limited to a single country
DGPS needs a nearby surveyed base station, and PPP does not
correct_answer: DGPS needs a nearby surveyed base station, and PPP does not
explanation: PPP takes precise orbit and clock products computed by a global monitoring network, so the receiver needs no local reference. DGPS depends on a base station close enough to share the same errors.
topic: GPS signal integration and augmentation in 5G-NTN

question_text: In DGPS, how is the correction value derived?
options: From the difference between the base station's surveyed position and its GPS-computed position
From the carrier phase difference between two satellites in view
From a model of ionospheric delay held at the master station
From averaging the positions reported by all nearby rovers
correct_answer: From the difference between the base station's surveyed position and its GPS-computed position
explanation: The base station already knows exactly where it is. Any disagreement between that truth and what GPS reports is the current error, and that error is what gets broadcast to nearby receivers.
topic: GPS signal integration and augmentation in 5G-NTN

question_text: Which technique reaches centimetre-level accuracy by using carrier-phase measurements between a base and a rover?
options: SBAS
RTK
DGPS
PPP
correct_answer: RTK
explanation: RTK is quoted at 1 to 2 cm. Carrier phase resolves position to a fraction of a wavelength, which is far finer than the code measurements DGPS relies on.
topic: GPS signal integration and augmentation in 5G-NTN

question_text: In SBAS, what does the geostationary satellite actually do?
options: It measures the GPS errors directly using its own receiver
It replaces a failed GPS satellite in the constellation
It broadcasts the correction messages that were computed on the ground
It relays the user position back to the master control station
correct_answer: It broadcasts the correction messages that were computed on the ground
explanation: The errors are detected by surveyed reference stations and turned into correction messages by a master control station. The GEO satellite is only the broadcast channel that carries them over a wide area.
topic: GPS signal integration and augmentation in 5G-NTN

question_text: A node transmits a positioning signal, the device replies, and the node halves the measured delay. Which technique is this?
options: Time of Arrival
Angle of Arrival
Trilateration from ephemeris
Round Trip Time
correct_answer: Round Trip Time
explanation: The halving is the giveaway. Measuring a two-way delay and dividing by two removes the need for the transmitter and the receiver to share a clock, which is what a one-way Time of Arrival measurement would require.
topic: GPS signal integration and augmentation in 5G-NTN

question_text: Angle of Arrival needs something that Time of Arrival does not. What?
options: An antenna array able to resolve the direction the signal came from
A precisely synchronised clock at the transmitter
Knowledge of the satellite ephemeris
A carrier-phase capable receiver
correct_answer: An antenna array able to resolve the direction the signal came from
explanation: AoA works on direction rather than distance, and direction is recovered from the phase differences across the elements of an array. A single antenna cannot tell you where a signal came from.
topic: GPS signal integration and augmentation in 5G-NTN

question_text: Why is 5G-NTN a useful complement to GPS in urban canyons and indoors?
options: NTN signals are transmitted at a much lower carrier frequency
NTN platforms supply extra measurements where the sky view is blocked
NTN removes the need for trilateration entirely
NTN satellites orbit lower and therefore penetrate buildings
correct_answer: NTN platforms supply extra measurements where the sky view is blocked
explanation: GPS fails in those places because too few satellites are visible. Adding ToA, AoA and RTT measurements from NTN platforms restores enough observations to solve for position.
topic: GPS signal integration and augmentation in 5G-NTN

question_text: SBAS is stated to improve accuracy from what range to what range?
options: From 1 to 3 metres down to about 20 centimetres
From 20 metres down to about 5 metres
From 5 to 10 metres down to about 1 to 2 metres
From 1 to 2 metres down to about 1 to 2 centimetres
correct_answer: From 5 to 10 metres down to about 1 to 2 metres
explanation: SBAS sits in the middle of the augmentation ladder. DGPS reaches 1 to 3 m, PPP about 5 to 20 cm after convergence, and RTK 1 to 2 cm.
topic: GPS signal integration and augmentation in 5G-NTN

question_text: Which statement about the user segment of GPS is correct?
options: It uploads corrected navigation messages to the satellites
It monitors satellite health and flags faulty spacecraft
It transmits a ranging signal back to the constellation
It consists of the receivers and the devices or people using them
correct_answer: It consists of the receivers and the devices or people using them
explanation: The user segment only listens. Uploading corrections and monitoring health are control segment jobs, and no GPS receiver transmits anything back to the satellites.
topic: GPS signal integration and augmentation in 5G-NTN

question_text: Why does the presentation argue that the two systems must be combined?
options: Neither GPS alone nor 5G alone gives good positioning in every condition
GPS can provide time but not position
5G-NTN cannot measure distance without GPS assistance
Augmentation schemes only work when both systems are present
correct_answer: Neither GPS alone nor 5G alone gives good positioning in every condition
explanation: GPS is strong under open sky and weak in canyons, tunnels and indoors. 5G-NTN covers places terrestrial networks cannot. The hybrid exists because the two failure modes do not overlap.
topic: GPS signal integration and augmentation in 5G-NTN

question_text: Why can an ordinary unmodified smartphone attach to a HAPS, when it cannot attach directly to most satellites?
options: A HAPS is a standard 5G base station flown at altitude, so the link budget closes to a handset
A HAPS transmits on unlicensed spectrum that all phones already support
A HAPS uses a modulation scheme designed specifically for handsets
Satellites do not implement the 5G NR air interface at all
correct_answer: A HAPS is a standard 5G base station flown at altitude, so the link budget closes to a handset
explanation: The deciding factor is distance. At about 20 km the path loss is small enough that a normal phone closes the link, which the deck quotes as roughly 28 dB better than a 500 km LEO.
topic: HAPS-based disaster recovery with 5G core integration

question_text: What does the local-breakout UPF on the HAPS payload achieve?
options: It authenticates responders without contacting the ground core
Responder traffic can be switched locally and never leaves the disaster zone
It stores traffic until the ground network is restored
It removes the need for a feeder link to the gateway
correct_answer: Responder traffic can be switched locally and never leaves the disaster zone
explanation: The User Plane Function is where user traffic is routed. Putting one on the platform means two responders in the same area can talk through the HAPS alone, without a round trip to the ground core.
topic: HAPS-based disaster recovery with 5G core integration

question_text: Which functions stay on the ground 5G core even with a regenerative HAPS payload?
options: Radio resource control and scheduling
Local user-plane switching between responders
Authentication and session management, and routing to external networks
Beamforming weight computation for the service link
correct_answer: Authentication and session management, and routing to external networks
explanation: The AMF and the SMF stay on the ground. The payload carries the gNB and a breakout UPF, so it handles the radio and local traffic, but subscriber authentication and external routing remain a core function.
topic: HAPS-based disaster recovery with 5G core integration

question_text: How does HAPS end-to-end latency compare with GEO in the quoted table?
options: Roughly the same, since both are line-of-sight links
HAPS is around one order of magnitude lower
HAPS is higher because of the extra gateway hop
HAPS is roughly fifty times lower
correct_answer: HAPS is roughly fifty times lower
explanation: The table gives 1 to 10 ms for HAPS against 480 to 560 ms for GEO. Comparing the middle of each range puts the ratio near fifty.
topic: HAPS-based disaster recovery with 5G core integration

question_text: What link-budget advantage is quoted for a 20 km HAPS over a 500 km LEO for direct-to-smartphone service?
options: About 28 dB
About 3 dB
About 12 dB
About 60 dB
correct_answer: About 28 dB
explanation: The figure follows from the range ratio. Being twenty-five times closer buys roughly 28 dB of path loss, which is what makes an unmodified handset viable.
topic: HAPS-based disaster recovery with 5G core integration

question_text: Which challenge belongs to the Ka-band feeder link rather than the service link?
options: Station-keeping against stratospheric winds
Rain fade, which has to be handled with site diversity
Airspace clearance for the platform
Sharing one platform's capacity across the whole footprint
correct_answer: Rain fade, which has to be handled with site diversity
explanation: Rain attenuation grows sharply with frequency, so a 20 to 30 GHz feeder link is vulnerable in a way the lower-frequency service link is not. Site diversity answers it by having a second gateway in different weather.
topic: HAPS-based disaster recovery with 5G core integration

question_text: A single HAPS covers a 50 to 100 km radius. What does that mean for capacity?
options: Capacity scales automatically with the radius covered
The radius must be reduced before the data rate can rise
One platform's capacity is shared across that entire footprint
Coverage beyond 50 km requires a second feeder link
correct_answer: One platform's capacity is shared across that entire footprint
explanation: Coverage and capacity are different quantities. A wide footprint is an advantage for reach and a disadvantage for throughput per user, because every user inside it draws on the same payload.
topic: HAPS-based disaster recovery with 5G core integration

question_text: Why is deployment speed the decisive advantage of HAPS in disaster response?
options: The platform can be recovered and reused after the event
It needs no gateway on the ground
It operates in spectrum permanently reserved for emergencies
It can be flown in hours or days, with no launch campaign
correct_answer: It can be flown in hours or days, with no launch campaign
explanation: A satellite has to be built, scheduled and launched. Disaster response is measured in hours, and a platform that can be in the air the same day is the only one that arrives while it still matters.
topic: HAPS-based disaster recovery with 5G core integration

question_text: Endurance is listed as an open problem. What figure is quoted?
options: 12 days is the current airship record
12 hours is the current airship record
12 weeks is the current airship record
12 months is the current airship record
correct_answer: 12 days is the current airship record
explanation: Twelve days is long enough for an emergency deployment and far short of permanent infrastructure, which is why the deck calls HAPS a temporary layer by design.
topic: HAPS-based disaster recovery with 5G core integration

question_text: The conclusion attaches a condition to the claim that HAPS restores coverage. What is it?
options: The terrestrial towers must be only partially damaged
Backhaul must survive through a gateway, a satellite or another HAPS
The handsets must be upgraded to support NTN
The disaster zone must be smaller than 50 km across
correct_answer: Backhaul must survive through a gateway, a satellite or another HAPS
explanation: A HAPS restores the radio access network, not the transport behind it. Without a surviving path to the core, the platform can connect phones to each other locally but not to anything beyond the zone.
topic: HAPS-based disaster recovery with 5G core integration

question_text: What distinguishes make-before-break handover from a conventional handover?
options: The old link is released before the new one is established
The new link is established before the old one is released
Both links are released and the device re-attaches from idle
The handover is decided by the device rather than the network
correct_answer: The new link is established before the old one is released
explanation: A conventional handover has a gap between releasing one link and acquiring the next. Overlapping the two removes that gap, which is what stops the session from dropping.
topic: Multi-connectivity and session continuity across TN-NTN links

question_text: A device is attached to a 5G base station and a LEO satellite at the same time. Which technology enables that?
options: Access Traffic Steering, Switching and Splitting
Network slicing
Multi-Radio Dual Connectivity
Multi-Access Edge Computing
correct_answer: Multi-Radio Dual Connectivity
explanation: MR-DC is the mechanism that lets one device hold simultaneous connections over two different radio accesses. ATSSS then decides what traffic to send over which of them.
topic: Multi-connectivity and session continuity across TN-NTN links

question_text: ATSSS and MR-DC are related but distinct. What does ATSSS add?
options: It creates the simultaneous radio connections in the first place
It authenticates the device on each access network separately
It predicts when a handover will become necessary
It decides how traffic is routed and balanced across the connections
correct_answer: It decides how traffic is routed and balanced across the connections
explanation: MR-DC provides the pipes and ATSSS provides the policy. Steering, switching and splitting are three ways of dividing a traffic flow across pipes that already exist.
topic: Multi-connectivity and session continuity across TN-NTN links

question_text: Which challenge is matched with intelligent routing as its solution?
options: Latency differences between the access types
Frequent handovers
Link failures
Session interruption
correct_answer: Latency differences between the access types
explanation: A satellite path and a terrestrial path have very different delays. Routing intelligently means sending delay-sensitive traffic down the short path and bulk traffic down the long one.
topic: Multi-connectivity and session continuity across TN-NTN links

question_text: Why does MEC help specifically during mobility?
options: It removes the need for a satellite feeder link
It processes data closer to the user, so latency stays low as the link changes
It stores the session context so the device need not re-authenticate
It selects which satellite the device should connect to next
correct_answer: It processes data closer to the user, so latency stays low as the link changes
explanation: Edge computing shortens the path between the user and the application. When the access link is switching between terrestrial and satellite, keeping the compute nearby limits how much the round trip can grow.
topic: Multi-connectivity and session continuity across TN-NTN links

question_text: How is session continuity defined?
options: A device stays attached to one satellite for a whole pass
A fixed data rate is reserved for the duration of a call
An ongoing session is preserved while the underlying link changes
Both terrestrial and satellite links are always kept available
correct_answer: An ongoing session is preserved while the underlying link changes
explanation: Continuity is about the session surviving, not about the link staying still. The benefits listed follow from that: no repeated logins, no data loss and a stable experience.
topic: Multi-connectivity and session continuity across TN-NTN links

question_text: How does network slicing contribute to seamless connectivity?
options: It reduces the number of handovers a device must perform
It splits a single session across two carriers to raise throughput
It pre-computes the beam weights for the satellite link
It gives each application a dedicated virtual network with consistent quality of service
correct_answer: It gives each application a dedicated virtual network with consistent quality of service
explanation: Slicing isolates services from one another, so a latency-critical application keeps its guarantees even when the network beneath it changes access type or comes under load.
topic: Multi-connectivity and session continuity across TN-NTN links

question_text: Which benefit belongs to multi-connectivity rather than to session continuity?
options: Load balancing and a backup path if one link fails
No repeated logins
No data loss during a link change
A stable experience for the end user
correct_answer: Load balancing and a backup path if one link fails
explanation: Load balancing and redundancy require two links running at once, which is what multi-connectivity provides. The other three are what continuity delivers once the link does change.
topic: Multi-connectivity and session continuity across TN-NTN links

question_text: Frequent handovers are listed as an NTN challenge. What causes them?
options: The high altitude of the satellite platform
LEO satellites sweep across the sky, so the serving cell keeps changing
Congestion in the terrestrial network
The mismatch in latency between the two access types
correct_answer: LEO satellites sweep across the sky, so the serving cell keeps changing
explanation: In a terrestrial network the user moves past fixed towers. In a LEO network the tower itself moves, so even a stationary user is handed over every few minutes.
topic: Multi-connectivity and session continuity across TN-NTN links

question_text: AI-assisted mobility management turns the handover from reactive into proactive. How?
options: By raising the signal strength threshold that triggers a handover
By handing over to the satellite whenever the terrestrial link weakens
By predicting user movement and network conditions ahead of time
By keeping the device on the terrestrial link for as long as possible
correct_answer: By predicting user movement and network conditions ahead of time
explanation: A reactive handover waits for a measurement to cross a threshold. Predicting the movement lets the network prepare the target in advance, so the switch happens before the link degrades.
topic: Multi-connectivity and session continuity across TN-NTN links

question_text: A PFD mask is expressed as a function of elevation angle. Why does the elevation angle matter?
options: The satellite transmits more power at low elevation
Doppler shift is largest at high elevation angles
It determines how much satellite energy reaches a terrestrial receiver at the surface
The terrestrial base station antenna tilts with elevation
correct_answer: It determines how much satellite energy reaches a terrestrial receiver at the surface
explanation: A beam arriving steeply from overhead spreads its energy differently from one arriving near the horizon, and terrestrial antennas discriminate against those angles differently. The regulatory limit therefore has to be angle dependent.
topic: Spectrum sharing and interference management between 5G NTN and TN

question_text: What does EPFD add beyond an ordinary PFD limit?
options: It applies the limit to the uplink as well as the downlink
It converts the limit into a time-averaged rather than a peak value
It extends the limit to adjacent bands as well as the co-channel band
It accounts for the aggregate interference from a whole constellation
correct_answer: It accounts for the aggregate interference from a whole constellation
explanation: A single spacecraft can comply while a constellation of hundreds, all visible at once, still swamps a terrestrial receiver. EPFD is the equivalent limit applied to the summed contribution.
topic: Spectrum sharing and interference management between 5G NTN and TN

question_text: Null-steering suppresses interference without simply reducing transmit power. How?
options: It places a null in the radiation pattern toward the victim receiver
It narrows the main lobe until it misses the victim receiver
It shifts the beam into an adjacent frequency band
It reduces the number of active antenna elements
correct_answer: It places a null in the radiation pattern toward the victim receiver
explanation: An adaptive array can shape its pattern, not just point it. Steering a null at the victim removes energy in that one direction while the main lobe keeps serving its intended users at full power.
topic: Spectrum sharing and interference management between 5G NTN and TN

question_text: Which interference mechanism arises purely from the speed of LEO satellites?
options: Co-channel interference
Doppler-induced spreading
Adjacent-band leakage
Cross-border coexistence
correct_answer: Doppler-induced spreading
explanation: The other three exist for a stationary satellite too. Only spectral smearing from a rapidly changing frequency offset is a direct consequence of orbital velocity.
topic: Spectrum sharing and interference management between 5G NTN and TN

question_text: In the uplink interference scenario, who is the victim?
options: A terrestrial user equipment inside the satellite footprint
The terrestrial base station, reached by the satellite downlink
The satellite receiver, reached by a terrestrial user's transmission
The gateway earth station on the feeder link
correct_answer: The satellite receiver, reached by a terrestrial user's transmission
explanation: Direction defines the victim. On the downlink the satellite beam spills into the terrestrial cell and a ground user suffers. On the uplink the terrestrial transmission rises into the satellite and the satellite suffers.
topic: Spectrum sharing and interference management between 5G NTN and TN

question_text: Which approach sits underneath dynamic spectrum sharing rather than beside it?
options: Exclusive or licensed allocation
Static co-primary sharing
Geographic separation using exclusion zones
Cognitive sensing
correct_answer: Cognitive sensing
explanation: The tree has four top-level approaches. Dynamic spectrum sharing then branches into power control, adaptive beamforming, cognitive sensing and AI/ML-based allocation.
topic: Spectrum sharing and interference management between 5G NTN and TN

question_text: Which 3GPP release is identified as the first NTN specification?
options: Release 17
Release 15
Release 18
Release 20
correct_answer: Release 17
explanation: Releases 15 and 16 were study items. Release 17 in 2022 is where NR-NTN and NB-IoT or eMTC over satellite were first specified rather than merely studied.
topic: Spectrum sharing and interference management between 5G NTN and TN

question_text: Why is cross-border regulation listed as an open challenge?
options: Satellites cannot switch frequency as they cross a border
Different countries have to agree on the same PFD rules
Terrestrial operators are not licensed to serve foreign users
Doppler shift changes as the satellite crosses a boundary
correct_answer: Different countries have to agree on the same PFD rules
explanation: A beam does not stop at a national boundary, but spectrum regulation does. Two neighbouring administrations with different limits leave the operator with no single rule to comply with.
topic: Spectrum sharing and interference management between 5G NTN and TN

question_text: When are guard bands and guard time slots used?
options: When the satellite must reduce its power flux density
When the constellation exceeds its EPFD budget
When co-channel sharing between NTN and TN is not workable
When the terrestrial network is congested
correct_answer: When co-channel sharing between NTN and TN is not workable
explanation: Guard resources are the fallback. They separate the two systems in frequency or in time and give up the efficiency that sharing the same resources would have provided.
topic: Spectrum sharing and interference management between 5G NTN and TN

question_text: The takeaways name one direction as the clear road to 6G. Which?
options: Exclusive licensed allocation for NTN
Wider guard bands between NTN and TN
Moving all NTN traffic into Ka-band
AI/ML-driven dynamic spectrum sharing
correct_answer: AI/ML-driven dynamic spectrum sharing
explanation: The other three all work by keeping the systems apart, which wastes spectrum. Learning to share the same spectrum in real time is what the deck identifies as the path forward.
topic: Spectrum sharing and interference management between 5G NTN and TN

question_text: Which RRC state keeps the UE context stored in the network while the connection itself is released?
options: RRC CONNECTED
RRC IDLE
RRC SETUP
RRC INACTIVE
correct_answer: RRC INACTIVE
explanation: INACTIVE is the middle state and it exists to make resuming cheap. IDLE keeps no context, so returning to CONNECTED from IDLE needs a full RRC setup.
topic: Mobility management and handover optimization in 5G NTN

question_text: Why is a purely signal-strength-based handover trigger inadequate in NTN?
options: The satellite keeps moving, so the measurement is out of date by the time it is acted on
Satellites do not transmit reference signals that can be measured
Signal strength cannot be measured through the ionosphere
The device has no way to report measurements on the uplink
correct_answer: The satellite keeps moving, so the measurement is out of date by the time it is acted on
explanation: A measurement report has to travel to the network and a decision has to travel back. Over a satellite link that takes long enough for the geometry that justified the report to have changed.
topic: Mobility management and handover optimization in 5G NTN

question_text: A time-based trigger fires at a predicted moment. Where does the prediction come from?
options: The historical measurement log stored in the device
Satellite ephemeris and orbit data
The current network load at the target satellite
The rate of change of the received signal strength
correct_answer: Satellite ephemeris and orbit data
explanation: Orbits are deterministic, so the time at which a given satellite will fall below a usable elevation can be computed in advance rather than waited for.
topic: Mobility management and handover optimization in 5G NTN

question_text: What distinguishes conditional handover from a location-based trigger on its own?
options: It uses no location information at all
It is executed by the device without network involvement
Several conditions have to be satisfied together before it fires
It always hands over to a beam on the same satellite
correct_answer: Several conditions have to be satisfied together before it fires
explanation: Location is one of the conditions in the set, alongside link quality, time to degradation and target load. Requiring all of them at once is what cuts unnecessary handovers.
topic: Mobility management and handover optimization in 5G NTN

question_text: Which condition in the conditional handover set concerns the target rather than the radio link?
options: Target SINR exceeds serving SINR plus a hysteresis margin
Time to link degradation is below a threshold
The UE is inside the target coverage area
The target satellite's load is below a maximum
correct_answer: The target satellite's load is below a maximum
explanation: Load is a capacity property of the target cell, not a property of the radio path. Checking it stops the network from handing a device onto a satellite that is already full.
topic: Mobility management and handover optimization in 5G NTN

question_text: How does beam-based handover differ from satellite handover?
options: The device switches between spot beams of the same satellite
The device has to change carrier frequency
It is triggered only by time and never by location
It removes the need for a timing advance update
correct_answer: The device switches between spot beams of the same satellite
explanation: A single satellite projects many spot beams, and the footprint of each sweeps across the ground. A user can leave one beam and enter another without ever changing satellite.
topic: Mobility management and handover optimization in 5G NTN

question_text: Reserving resources at the target satellite before a handover carries which specific cost?
options: The device battery drains from continuous location fixing
Capacity is wasted whenever the handover does not actually take place
Doppler pre-compensation becomes impossible
The RRC state has to fall back to IDLE
correct_answer: Capacity is wasted whenever the handover does not actually take place
explanation: Preparing in advance means committing resources on a prediction. Every prediction that does not come true has held capacity idle that could have served someone else.
topic: Mobility management and handover optimization in 5G NTN

question_text: Why does a location-based trigger drain the device battery?
options: It requires the device to stay in RRC CONNECTED at all times
It doubles the number of transmit chains in use
The device has to keep obtaining position fixes
It forces the device to measure every visible satellite
correct_answer: The device has to keep obtaining position fixes
explanation: Knowing when a geographic boundary has been crossed means knowing where you are continuously. A GNSS receiver running all the time is a significant, constant power draw.
topic: Mobility management and handover optimization in 5G NTN

question_text: Make-before-break is described as adding hardware complexity. Why?
options: The device has to store the full ephemeris of the constellation
The satellite has to carry an additional soft buffer
The device has to run an AI model in real time
The device has to support two simultaneous links
correct_answer: The device has to support two simultaneous links
explanation: Holding the old link while the new one comes up means two active radio connections at once, which needs the receive and transmit hardware to support both.
topic: Mobility management and handover optimization in 5G NTN

question_text: How does the conclusion characterise the overall shift in NTN mobility management?
options: From reactive and signal-based to predictive and ephemeris-driven
From ephemeris-driven to measurement-driven
From network-controlled to device-controlled
From beam-based to satellite-based handover
correct_answer: From reactive and signal-based to predictive and ephemeris-driven
explanation: The old model waits for a measurement to degrade. The new one exploits the fact that satellite motion is known in advance, and pays for that with signalling, battery and reserved capacity.
topic: Mobility management and handover optimization in 5G NTN

question_text: What is the defining feature of Integrated Sensing and Communication?
options: One waveform, one RF front end and one slice of spectrum serve both functions
A radar payload is flown alongside a communication payload on one satellite
Sensing data is carried as payload traffic over the communication link
A communication link switches between data and radar modes in turn
correct_answer: One waveform, one RF front end and one slice of spectrum serve both functions
explanation: The integration is in the hardware and the waveform, not in the packaging. Two payloads on one bus, or time-sharing one link, both keep the functions separate; ISAC does not.
topic: ISAC-enabled non-terrestrial networks for 6G

question_text: Why is a GEO satellite ranged rather than tracked by Doppler?
options: GEO satellites transmit at a frequency too high for Doppler processing
GEO shows almost no Doppler because it is nearly stationary relative to the ground
GEO Doppler is masked by ionospheric scintillation
GEO orbits are known exactly, so no tracking is needed at all
correct_answer: GEO shows almost no Doppler because it is nearly stationary relative to the ground
explanation: Doppler needs relative radial motion. A geostationary satellite holds its position over a point on the ground, so the shift is close to zero and there is no signature to track.
topic: ISAC-enabled non-terrestrial networks for 6G

question_text: In a multistatic ISAC configuration, what is the arrangement?
options: Each satellite transmits and listens for its own echo
One satellite transmits and a single second satellite receives the reflection
One transmission is received by several nodes across the constellation
The ground station transmits and the satellites all receive
correct_answer: One transmission is received by several nodes across the constellation
explanation: The deck shows one transmitter and receivers Rx1 through Rx4 all catching the same echo. Many viewing angles on one target is what turns the constellation itself into a radar.
topic: ISAC-enabled non-terrestrial networks for 6G

question_text: Self-interference is a problem in which geometry, and why?
options: Bistatic, because the two nodes are not synchronised
Multistatic, because several echoes arrive at once
All three equally, because the waveform is shared
Monostatic, because the receiver must hear a faint echo through its own loud transmitter
correct_answer: Monostatic, because the receiver must hear a faint echo through its own loud transmitter
explanation: Sharing one aperture means transmitting and receiving at the same time and place. The returning echo is many orders of magnitude weaker than the outgoing signal sitting on top of it.
topic: ISAC-enabled non-terrestrial networks for 6G

question_text: Roughly how much cancellation is quoted as necessary for the monostatic case?
options: More than 70 dB
More than 20 dB
More than 40 dB
More than 120 dB
correct_answer: More than 70 dB
explanation: The deck specifies more than 70 dB of combined analog and digital cancellation, and notes that it has to be achieved on a moving payload, which makes it harder still.
topic: ISAC-enabled non-terrestrial networks for 6G

question_text: What is the principal challenge that bistatic and multistatic operation introduces, and that monostatic avoids?
options: Self-interference between transmit and receive
Time and phase synchronisation across independent nodes
The need for a joint waveform design
The absence of a native ISAC standard
correct_answer: Time and phase synchronisation across independent nodes
explanation: One aperture shares one clock by construction. Splitting transmit from receive across separate spacecraft means those spacecraft have to agree on time and phase to sub-microsecond accuracy.
topic: ISAC-enabled non-terrestrial networks for 6G

question_text: Why does limited onboard power and compute add latency to ISAC over NTN?
options: The waveform has to be transmitted at a lower rate
The receiver must integrate over a longer dwell time
Processing is pushed down to the ground rather than done on board
The satellite must store echoes until it passes a gateway
correct_answer: Processing is pushed down to the ground rather than done on board
explanation: If the payload cannot process the returns itself, the raw data has to be downlinked and processed on the ground, and the answer comes back a full round trip later.
topic: ISAC-enabled non-terrestrial networks for 6G

question_text: Which advantage follows directly from not needing dedicated sensing spectrum?
options: High-precision localization
Extreme disaster resilience
Real-time environment mapping
Enhanced spectral efficiency and reduced congestion
correct_answer: Enhanced spectral efficiency and reduced congestion
explanation: Conventional radar occupies a band that carries no data. Folding the sensing into the communication waveform frees that allocation, which is a spectrum-efficiency gain rather than a capability gain.
topic: ISAC-enabled non-terrestrial networks for 6G

question_text: In the maritime use case, what is meant by one beam doing two jobs?
options: The beam tracks ships and reads sea state while also serving broadband
The beam serves two vessels at the same time
The beam alternates between uplink and downlink
The beam covers both the coastline and the open ocean
correct_answer: The beam tracks ships and reads sea state while also serving broadband
explanation: The two jobs are sensing and communication, not two users or two directions. Over water there are no towers, so the same beam has to earn its place twice.
topic: ISAC-enabled non-terrestrial networks for 6G

question_text: DebriSense-THz is quoted with which performance figure?
options: 70 dB of interference cancellation at 5 THz
95 to 99 percent classification accuracy at 5 THz
Sub-microsecond synchronisation at 5 THz
95 to 99 percent spectral efficiency gain at 5 THz
correct_answer: 95 to 99 percent classification accuracy at 5 THz
explanation: The figure belongs to the space situational awareness use case: detecting, tracking and classifying orbiting debris, where classification accuracy is the metric that matters.
topic: ISAC-enabled non-terrestrial networks for 6G

question_text: What separates the Non-RT RIC from the Near-RT RIC?
options: The Non-RT RIC runs on the satellite and the Near-RT RIC on the ground
The Non-RT RIC runs loops slower than one second and the Near-RT RIC faster than one second
The Non-RT RIC handles user data and the Near-RT RIC handles control signalling
The Non-RT RIC is vendor-specific and the Near-RT RIC is open
correct_answer: The Non-RT RIC runs loops slower than one second and the Near-RT RIC faster than one second
explanation: The split is by control-loop timescale. Slow work such as policy and model training goes above one second; fast optimisation through xApps goes below it.
topic: AI-native Open RAN for NTN

question_text: Which functions sit in the O-CU-CP?
options: RLC and MAC
SDAP and PDCP
RRC and PDCP
High-PHY and Low-PHY
correct_answer: RRC and PDCP
explanation: The control-plane half of the central unit carries RRC together with PDCP. SDAP with PDCP is the user-plane half, and RLC with MAC belongs to the distributed unit.
topic: AI-native Open RAN for NTN

question_text: What is the main structural difference between traditional RAN and Open RAN?
options: Open RAN removes the need for a core network
Open RAN places all processing in the radio unit
Open RAN uses satellites instead of ground towers
Open RAN splits the chain into functions that may come from different vendors
correct_answer: Open RAN splits the chain into functions that may come from different vendors
explanation: A traditional RAN is a single vendor's baseband unit and radio unit joined by proprietary interfaces. Open RAN standardises those interfaces so O-CU, O-DU and O-RU can be sourced separately.
topic: AI-native Open RAN for NTN

question_text: In the AI-RAN model, which layer covers AI hardware, AI software and AI integration used to improve the network itself?
options: AI-for-RAN
AI-on-RAN
AI-and-RAN
AI-over-RAN
correct_answer: AI-for-RAN
explanation: The three layers are concentric. AI-for-RAN is the innermost and points inward at the network. AI-and-RAN shares infrastructure, and AI-on-RAN sells services outward over the network.
topic: AI-native Open RAN for NTN

question_text: AI-on-RAN is best described as:
options: Using AI to optimize scheduling inside the base station
Delivering AI services to customers over the network
Sharing infrastructure between AI workloads and RAN workloads
Training AI models on the satellite payload
correct_answer: Delivering AI services to customers over the network
explanation: It is the outermost layer, covering the marketplace platform, developer tools and global access. The network becomes the delivery channel for AI rather than the thing being optimised.
topic: AI-native Open RAN for NTN

question_text: Which component actually allocates satellite beams and resources to user devices in the described NTN pipeline?
options: The Service Management and Orchestration framework
rApps running on the Non-RT RIC
xApps running on the Near-RT RIC
The O-RU on board the satellite
correct_answer: xApps running on the Near-RT RIC
explanation: The machine learning engine predicts and optimises, but the allocation itself is a fast control action, and fast control actions are what xApps on the Near-RT RIC exist to perform.
topic: AI-native Open RAN for NTN

question_text: Why does satellite mobility create a problem for Open RAN specifically?
options: Open interfaces cannot carry ephemeris data
The O-Cloud cannot be deployed on a moving platform
xApps must be recompiled for each orbital plane
O-RAN interfaces assume a static fronthaul with predictable latency
correct_answer: O-RAN interfaces assume a static fronthaul with predictable latency
explanation: The functional splits were designed for a fibre run of known length between a baseband unit and a radio unit. A moving satellite changes that path length continuously, which breaks the timing assumption.
topic: AI-native Open RAN for NTN

question_text: The RIC placement question in NTN is a choice between:
options: The ground segment and the satellite
The core network and the radio unit
The Non-RT RIC and the Near-RT RIC
A single vendor and multiple vendors
correct_answer: The ground segment and the satellite
explanation: Putting the RIC on the ground keeps compute cheap and adds a round trip to every decision. Putting it on the satellite removes the round trip and spends scarce onboard power.
topic: AI-native Open RAN for NTN

question_text: Which AI application is described as using signal strength, network load and user motion together?
options: Beam optimization
Intelligent handover
Self-optimizing network operations
Functional split selection
correct_answer: Intelligent handover
explanation: Those three inputs feed the handover decision, so the network can choose the best target satellite along an intelligent prediction path rather than reacting to one measurement.
topic: AI-native Open RAN for NTN

question_text: The claim that resource optimization gets harder after deployment rests on which fact?
options: The constellation grows over time as more satellites are launched
The AI model degrades as its training data ages
The geometry keeps changing once the constellation is flying
Open interfaces cannot be updated after deployment
correct_answer: The geometry keeps changing once the constellation is flying
explanation: A terrestrial network is planned once and then largely holds still. A constellation never holds still, so the optimisation problem is re-posed continuously rather than solved at planning time.
topic: AI-native Open RAN for NTN

question_text: What does channel state information tell the satellite, and why does it have to be reported?
options: Which satellite the device intends to hand over to next
The device's GNSS position, so the beam can be pointed at it
How the radio path changes the signal, which the satellite needs before it can aim a beam
How much buffer the device has left for incoming data
correct_answer: How the radio path changes the signal, which the satellite needs before it can aim a beam
explanation: CSI describes the channel in strength and timing. The satellite cannot observe the downlink channel itself, so the device has to measure it and report it back before precoding is possible.
topic: Federated learning for CSI feedback and beam management in LEO NTN

question_text: In the conventional cycle the device measures, quantises, reports and the gNB precodes. What is the stated cost of that cycle?
options: Each report has to be acknowledged by the satellite before the next one
The device has to re-authenticate at the start of every reporting cycle
Quantisation forces the device to transmit at maximum power
The report must be repeated often, and its cost grows with antennas, users and report rate
correct_answer: The report must be repeated often, and its cost grows with antennas, users and report rate
explanation: The report is small on its own but it is sent constantly, by every user, and it grows with the size of the antenna array. Multiplied out, it becomes the dominant uplink load.
topic: Federated learning for CSI feedback and beam management in LEO NTN

question_text: Challenge one is that the report is stale on arrival. What makes it stale?
options: The satellite moves at about 7.5 km/s, so the channel changes between measurement and use
The report is queued behind higher-priority traffic in the uplink buffer
The codebook entry has to be looked up on the ground before use
The device only measures the channel once per connection
correct_answer: The satellite moves at about 7.5 km/s, so the channel changes between measurement and use
explanation: The deck lays the timeline out as measure, send, arrive, applied. The interval over which the channel stays valid is shorter than the measure-to-use delay, so the report describes a channel that has gone.
topic: Federated learning for CSI feedback and beam management in LEO NTN

question_text: Challenge two is that the data needed to fix the problem is private. Why is CSI private?
options: CSI reports include the subscriber identity in the header
A channel measurement is nearly unique to one place, so it identifies where a user is
The codebook index reveals which services the user is running
CSI is transmitted without ciphering on the uplink
correct_answer: A channel measurement is nearly unique to one place, so it identifies where a user is
explanation: The deck shows a measured CSI grid being turned back into a position. The multipath signature of a location acts as a fingerprint, so collecting raw CSI centrally exposes subscriber location.
topic: Federated learning for CSI feedback and beam management in LEO NTN

question_text: What does the learned encoder achieve, and what compression ratios are quoted?
options: It removes the need for any uplink report at all
It encrypts the CSI so the aggregator cannot read it, at ratios from 1/2 to 1/8
It compresses the CSI into a short codeword, at ratios from 1/16 to 1/64
It predicts the next CSI report, at ratios from 1/4 to 1/16
correct_answer: It compresses the CSI into a short codeword, at ratios from 1/16 to 1/64
explanation: An autoencoder is trained as a pair: an encoder on the device and a decoder at the gateway. Only the codeword crosses the link, which is where the 1/16 to 1/64 saving comes from.
topic: Federated learning for CSI feedback and beam management in LEO NTN

question_text: Why must the encoder and the decoder be trained together as one pair?
options: Training them separately would exceed the device's memory budget
3GPP requires joint training for all air-interface models
Separate training would make the codeword longer than the raw report
The decoder has to learn to invert the specific representation that the encoder produces
correct_answer: The decoder has to learn to invert the specific representation that the encoder produces
explanation: The codeword is not a standard format. It is whatever internal representation the encoder settles on, so only a decoder trained alongside it can reconstruct the channel from it.
topic: Federated learning for CSI feedback and beam management in LEO NTN

question_text: What is the defining property of federated learning in this design?
options: Model updates cross the link while the raw CSI never leaves the device
Each device trains a completely separate model that is never combined
Training happens only on the satellite, using data it collects itself
The global model is broadcast but never updated after deployment
correct_answer: Model updates cross the link while the raw CSI never leaves the device
explanation: Devices train locally on their own data and send only the resulting updates. The aggregator averages those updates, so it improves a shared model without ever holding anyone's raw measurements.
topic: Federated learning for CSI feedback and beam management in LEO NTN

question_text: Which algorithms are named as what the aggregator runs?
options: DQN, DDPG, PPO and SAC
FedAvg, FedProx, SCAFFOLD and FedAdam
FedAvg, Q-learning, LSTM and SGD
AES, Kyber, Dilithium and SHA-256
correct_answer: FedAvg, FedProx, SCAFFOLD and FedAdam
explanation: These are federated aggregation methods: FedAvg is the baseline, FedProx handles uneven data, SCAFFOLD corrects drift and FedAdam is an adaptive server. The other lists are reinforcement learning and cryptography.
topic: Federated learning for CSI feedback and beam management in LEO NTN

question_text: Where does putting the aggregator on the satellite sit in the trade-off?
options: It is the slowest option but it uses no onboard power
It removes the need for secure aggregation
It is the fastest option and it costs onboard power
It stops the satellite from being visible for longer than a few minutes
correct_answer: It is the fastest option and it costs onboard power
explanation: Ground-assisted aggregation makes every round cross the whole link. Aggregating on the satellite removes that trip, which is why it is fastest, and spends scarce payload power doing it.
topic: Federated learning for CSI feedback and beam management in LEO NTN

question_text: Applying the same idea to beam management replaces an exhaustive sweep with what?
options: A fixed beam schedule computed once at deployment
A request to the user device to nominate its preferred beam
A random beam selection that is corrected by the closed loop
A predictor fed by ephemeris and past beams that outputs the best beam directly
correct_answer: A predictor fed by ephemeris and past beams that outputs the best beam directly
explanation: In the sweep the device measures every beam and reports the best. With a predictor it measures once to confirm the prediction, which is where the reporting overhead is saved.
topic: Federated learning for CSI feedback and beam management in LEO NTN

question_text: Why does a fixed beam plan go out of date within seconds in a LEO network?
options: The user devices move too fast for a fixed plan to track
The subcarrier spacing changes as the elevation angle changes
Beam weights are erased whenever the satellite passes into eclipse
The cell itself moves at orbital speed, so the footprint has shifted
correct_answer: The cell itself moves at orbital speed, so the footprint has shifted
explanation: In a terrestrial network the cell is fixed and the users move. In LEO the reverse dominates: the beam footprint sweeps the ground at kilometres per second, so any plan set in advance is stale immediately.
topic: AI-driven dynamic beam control for LEO 5G-NTN

question_text: The deck shows some cells at high demand and others at low or no demand under a uniform power allocation. What problem does this illustrate?
options: Highly dynamic and uneven traffic wastes resources on empty cells
Co-channel interference between adjacent beams
Timing misalignment between the SSB and the PRACH
Doppler spreading across the beam footprint
correct_answer: Highly dynamic and uneven traffic wastes resources on empty cells
explanation: Applying the same power to all cells means the busy cells are underserved while the empty ones consume payload resources that produce nothing.
topic: AI-driven dynamic beam control for LEO 5G-NTN

question_text: In the scheduling conflict shown, two cells both need the beam during mandatory signalling. What is the consequence?
options: Both cells receive the beam at half power
One of the cells is left with a coverage hole
The satellite defers the signalling to the next orbit
The devices in both cells fall back to a terrestrial carrier
correct_answer: One of the cells is left with a coverage hole
explanation: SSB and PRACH occupancy is fixed by the standard, so the beam cannot serve both cells at that instant. Whichever cell loses the contest is not covered when it needs to be.
topic: AI-driven dynamic beam control for LEO 5G-NTN

question_text: Under spatial-domain beam control, what is user-beam mapping for?
options: Assigning each user a unique preamble within the beam
Deciding which users are handed over to the next satellite
Grouping users by location so co-channel interference across adjacent beams is minimised
Matching each user to a network slice
correct_answer: Grouping users by location so co-channel interference across adjacent beams is minimised
explanation: How users are grouped into beams decides which of them end up sharing a frequency with a neighbouring beam. Grouping by location keeps reuse distances sensible.
topic: AI-driven dynamic beam control for LEO 5G-NTN

question_text: What is footprint shaping intended to compensate for?
options: Rain fade on the feeder link
The reversal of Doppler sign at the zenith
Uneven battery discharge across the payload
Changing slant range as the satellite moves from horizon to zenith
correct_answer: Changing slant range as the satellite moves from horizon to zenith
explanation: A beam of fixed angular width covers a much larger and more distorted ground area near the horizon than overhead. Widening or narrowing it keeps the covered area consistent through the pass.
topic: AI-driven dynamic beam control for LEO 5G-NTN

question_text: Beam hopping is a time-domain technique. What does it do?
options: It time-multiplexes physical beams across several ground cells to serve sporadic demand
It moves a beam to a new frequency when interference is detected
It switches a user between two satellites without a handover
It reshapes the beam as the slant range changes
correct_answer: It time-multiplexes physical beams across several ground cells to serve sporadic demand
explanation: With fewer beams than cells, the way to serve them all is to visit each in turn. Cells with more traffic are visited more often, which is how sporadic demand is met efficiently.
topic: AI-driven dynamic beam control for LEO 5G-NTN

question_text: What is signalling alignment concerned with?
options: Aligning the beam boresight with the user's GNSS position
Reserving the 3GPP-defined slots for synchronisation and broadcast so they do not collide with data
Matching the uplink and downlink frame timing at the gateway
Synchronising the phase of the elements in the antenna array
correct_answer: Reserving the 3GPP-defined slots for synchronisation and broadcast so they do not collide with data
explanation: Signals such as the SSB have to appear at defined times. The hopping schedule must work around those reservations rather than through them.
topic: AI-driven dynamic beam control for LEO 5G-NTN

question_text: In the 3GPP AI execution models, what characterises Type 3?
options: Joint training at one side only
Joint training at two sides using forward activation and backward gradient
Separate training at two sides, with a training dataset shared between them
Training performed entirely on the satellite payload
correct_answer: Separate training at two sides, with a training dataset shared between them
explanation: Type 1 trains at one side. Type 2 trains jointly across both sides by exchanging activations and gradients. Type 3 keeps the training separate and shares a dataset instead.
topic: AI-driven dynamic beam control for LEO 5G-NTN

question_text: Which limitation is stated as making a beam prediction error highly visible?
options: A wrong prediction raises the collision rate on the RACH
A wrong prediction forces the satellite into a safe mode
A wrong prediction increases the reporting overhead on the uplink
An incorrect prediction cuts coverage completely and causes a visible outage
correct_answer: An incorrect prediction cuts coverage completely and causes a visible outage
explanation: Beams are narrow and directional. Aiming one at the wrong place does not merely degrade service in that cell, it removes it, and the users there see a complete outage.
topic: AI-driven dynamic beam control for LEO 5G-NTN

question_text: What does the conclusion identify as the central engineering trade-off of AI-driven beam control?
options: Efficiency is bought with onboard computing power
Coverage is bought with additional spectrum
Latency is bought with a longer cyclic prefix
Reliability is bought with a larger constellation
correct_answer: Efficiency is bought with onboard computing power
explanation: Steering beams where capacity is actually needed raises efficiency, and the prediction that makes it possible has to run on a payload with a hard power and thermal budget.
topic: AI-driven dynamic beam control for LEO 5G-NTN

question_text: A GNSS receiver needs a minimum of four satellites rather than three. What does the fourth one resolve?
options: The receiver's own clock bias
The ambiguity between two candidate points in space
The ionospheric delay along each path
The identity of the constellation being tracked
correct_answer: The receiver's own clock bias
explanation: Three ranges fix a point in three dimensions if the clocks agree. A consumer receiver has no atomic clock, so its offset is a fourth unknown and needs a fourth equation.
topic: GPS and Galileo

question_text: Why is a pseudorange called pseudo?
options: It is measured to a predicted satellite position rather than the real one
It contains the receiver's time-synchronisation error, so it is not the true physical distance
It is derived from carrier phase rather than from the ranging code
It is an average over several satellites rather than a single measurement
correct_answer: It contains the receiver's time-synchronisation error, so it is not the true physical distance
explanation: The receiver converts travel time into distance using its own imperfect clock. That clock error appears in the result as an offset common to every satellite, which is what the fourth measurement removes.
topic: GPS and Galileo

question_text: A one microsecond clock error produces roughly what positioning error on the ground?
options: About 3 metres
About 30 metres
About 300 metres
About 3 kilometres
correct_answer: About 300 metres
explanation: Distance is the speed of light multiplied by time, and light travels about 300 metres in a microsecond. This is why the satellites carry atomic clocks accurate to nanoseconds.
topic: GPS and Galileo

question_text: How do GPS satellites share the same frequencies without interfering?
options: Each transmits in a different time slot on a rotating schedule
Each is allocated a narrow sub-band within the L1 carrier
Each transmits only when it is above a set elevation angle
Each transmits a unique pseudo-random noise code, so the receiver separates them by code
correct_answer: Each transmits a unique pseudo-random noise code, so the receiver separates them by code
explanation: This is code division multiple access. All the satellites occupy the same spectrum at once, and the receiver correlates against a known PRN code to pull out one satellite at a time.
topic: GPS and Galileo

question_text: Ephemeris and almanac data are both broadcast. What is the difference?
